s: Situation: one sentence of context (project, team, deadline).
Task: what you owned. Say 'I', not 'we'.
Action: two or three concrete steps you took, with the technical detail.
Result: a number if you have one (bugs found, weeks saved, tape-out met), then what you learned.
Keep it under 2 minutes. Prepare 5 stories in advance and reuse them.

project.t: Project deep dive: lead with a block diagram
s: Start with the one-line purpose and your exact role (what you designed or verified yourself).
Draw the block diagram: interfaces, clocks, data width, throughput.
Pick the hardest problem: a bug, a timing path, a coverage hole. Explain how you found and fixed it.
Give numbers: frequency, area, test count, coverage, bugs found.
Expect follow-ups on every word on your resume. Know why you made each choice.
List the features from the spec, then the checks for each feature.
Stimulus: directed tests for the basics, constrained random for the rest.
Checking: a reference model or scoreboard, plus assertions on the protocol.
Corner cases: empty/full, reset in the middle, back-to-back, max/min values, errors.
Close with coverage: functional coverage on features, code coverage to find holes.

flow.t: Flow question: stages, inputs, outputs, checks
s: Name the stages in order (e.g. RTL, synthesis, floorplan, place, CTS, route, signoff).
For each stage give the input files, the output and the main check (lint, STA, DRC/LVS, IR).
Mention one real problem you met at a stage and how it was fixed.
Finish with what decides sign-off: timing, power, physical checks, equivalence.
Draw it clean and big; label every node, terminal and axis.
Walk through it region by region (or input by input) out loud.
Mark the key numbers: threshold, gain, cut-off, delay.
Say what changes if a parameter changes (load, size, temperature).
Ask about input size, types and edge cases before writing.
Say the simple solution first, then improve it; state time and space complexity.
Write clean code with good names; talk while you write.
Test it by hand on a normal case and two edge cases (empty, one element, maximum).
Restate the problem and write down what is given.
Write the formula before plugging in numbers.
Check units and sanity: is the answer in a sensible range?
If unsure, say your assumption; interviewers mark the method more than the number.
Ask for the requirements: throughput, latency, widths, clocks, reset, area or power target.
Draw a block diagram, then the interfaces and the timing of one transaction.
Pick the hard part (control FSM, hazard, clock crossing) and detail it.
Discuss trade-offs and how you would verify it.

concept.t: Concept question: define, why, example, trade-off
s: One-line definition first.
Why it exists: the problem it solves.
A small example or diagram (a circuit, a waveform, a code snippet).
The trade-off or failure mode, and where you have seen it in real designs.

questions.q: What happens if you put the NMOS on top and the PMOS at the bottom of an inverter?
questions.st: AMD Dft Engineer Dallas Tx interview
questions.a: The circuit no longer works as a proper inverter. An NMOS passes a good 0 but only a weak 1 (it turns off once its source reaches VDD - Vtn), and a PMOS passes a good 1 but only a weak 0 (it stops at |Vtp| above ground). With NMOS on top and PMOS at the bottom, both act as source followers: the output swings only between about |Vtp| and VDD - Vtn, and it follows the input instead of inverting it. Noise margins collapse and the next gate may see an invalid level.

questions.q: Explain virtual memory and out-of-order execution.
questions.st: AMD Design Verification Engineer Boxborough Ma interview
questions.a: Virtual memory gives every process its own large, contiguous address space. The MMU translates virtual pages to physical frames using page tables cached in a TLB, so programs are isolated, memory can be over-committed, and pages can live on disk until used. Out-of-order execution lets a CPU execute instructions as soon as their operands are ready instead of in program order: instructions are renamed, wait in reservation stations, execute when ready and retire in order from a reorder buffer, so exceptions stay precise while stalls on long-latency loads are hidden.

questions.q: For a two-way set-associative cache of a given size, what do the bits of a memory address represent?

questions.q: How do MSHRs coalesce loads and stores to the same cache block?
questions.st: AMD Design Verification Intern Fishkill New York interview
questions.a: An MSHR (miss status holding register) tracks each outstanding cache miss. When a second load or store misses on a block that already has an MSHR, the cache does not send another request to memory; it records the new access (offset, size, destination register, store data) as an extra target in the same MSHR. When the line returns, the cache fills it once, merges any pending store data, and replies to every waiting load. This saves bandwidth and lets the core keep issuing while misses are in flight.

questions.q: How do you classify a workload as CPU-bound or memory-bound, with and without changing the microarchitecture?
questions.st: AMD Cpu Performance Modeling Engineer India interview
questions.a: Look at where cycles go. With performance counters: high IPC, low cache-miss and low memory-bandwidth use mean CPU-bound; many last-level misses, high average load latency, stalls on memory and bandwidth near peak mean memory-bound. A roofline view helps: compute the workload's operations per byte and compare with the machine's balance point. Without changing the microarchitecture, vary the core clock: runtime that scales with frequency is CPU-bound; runtime that barely changes is memory-bound. With microarchitecture changes, grow caches or memory bandwidth versus execution width and see which helps.

questions.q: How would you verify a write-back 4-way set-associative cache using assembly programs?
questions.st: AMD Design Verification Engineer Sunnyvale Ca interview

questions.q: On a multicore system with fixed memory architecture, how does single-core performance change as identical single-threaded workloads are scheduled on more cores?
questions.st: AMD Cpu Performance Modeling Engineer India interview
questions.a: Each additional copy competes for shared resources: last-level cache capacity, memory bandwidth, the interconnect and power or thermal headroom. Per-core performance stays flat while the working sets fit and bandwidth is plentiful, then drops as copies evict each other's data from the shared cache and memory bandwidth saturates. Turbo frequency also falls as more cores are active. Compute-bound workloads scale almost linearly; memory-bound ones show per-core throughput falling and total throughput flattening.

questions.q: What are pipeline hazards and how are they overcome?
questions.st: AMD Cpu Performance Modeling Engineer India interview
questions.a: Hazards stop the next instruction from executing in its planned cycle. Structural hazards: two instructions need the same resource (fix by duplicating it or stalling). Data hazards: an instruction needs a result not yet written (RAW; fix with forwarding/bypassing, stalls for load-use cases, and in out-of-order cores renaming removes WAR and WAW). Control hazards: the next PC is unknown after a branch (fix with branch prediction, early branch resolution, and flushing on a mispredict).

questions.q: What is the difference between shared memory and message passing?
questions.st: AMD Design Verification United States interview
questions.a: In shared memory, threads or cores communicate by reading and writing a common address space; it is easy to program but needs synchronisation (locks, atomics) and cache coherence hardware, and it scales less well. In message passing, each processor has private memory and communicates by explicitly sending and receiving messages (for example MPI or mailboxes); there is no coherence problem and it scales to many nodes, but data movement is explicit and the programming effort is higher.

questions.q: What is the disadvantage of higher cache associativity?
questions.st: AMD Verification Engineer Fort Collins Co interview
questions.a: Higher associativity reduces conflict misses, but every lookup must compare more tags in parallel. That costs area and power (more comparators and wider tag reads), and adds delay to the hit path through the larger way-select multiplexer, which can lower the clock frequency or add a pipeline stage. Replacement policy also gets more expensive (true LRU state grows quickly). Beyond 8 to 16 ways the miss-rate gain is usually small.

questions.q: What is virtual memory? What is a cache?
questions.st: AMD Hardware Intern New Delhi interview

questions.q: What types of caches are there?
questions.st: AMD Senior Asic Design Verification Engineer Boxborough Ma interview
questions.a: By organisation: direct-mapped (one place per address), set-associative (n places), fully associative (anywhere). By content: instruction, data and unified caches. By level: L1, L2, L3 (larger and slower further out), often private L1/L2 per core and a shared L3. By write policy: write-through or write-back, with write-allocate or no-write-allocate. There are also special caches such as the TLB, branch target buffer and micro-op cache. The choice trades hit time against miss rate.

questions.q: A disc is half white, half black. Design a digital circuit that detects whether it rotates clockwise or counterclockwise.
questions.st: AMD Asic Design Toronto On interview
questions.a: Use two sensors placed a little apart around the disc, for example 90 degrees in phase, so they produce two square waves A and B in quadrature (like a rotary encoder). Sample both with the clock and look at the order of edges: if A rises while B is 0, the disc turns one way; if A rises while B is 1, it turns the other way. A small FSM or a flop on each signal plus XOR logic gives a direction bit and can also count steps.

questions.q: A gate in a logic circuit is stuck at 1. What test inputs would show that the gate is defective?
questions.st: AMD Asic Design Engineer Coop Markham On interview
questions.a: To detect a stuck-at-1 on a gate output, you must excite the fault and propagate it. Excite: apply inputs that make the fault-free gate output 0 (for an AND, at least one input 0; for an OR, all inputs 0). Propagate: set the other inputs of each downstream gate to non-controlling values (1 for AND/NAND, 0 for OR/NOR) so the output difference reaches a primary output. If the observed output differs from the expected value, the gate is defective. The D-algorithm and ATPG tools automate this.

questions.q: A router must keep packets to the same address in order, while packets to different addresses may overtake each other. Packets carry no ID. How would you verify it?
questions.st: AMD Design Verification Engineer San Francisco Ca interview
questions.a: Build a scoreboard with one ordered queue per destination address. The monitor on the input side pushes each packet (its payload, since there is no ID) into the queue for its address; the output monitor pops the head of the queue for that address and compares. Any packet that matches a later entry instead of the head is an ordering error for the same address, while packets for different addresses are free to interleave. Drive random traffic with many packets to few addresses, back-pressure, and bursts, and add coverage on overtaking between different addresses.

questions.q: Explain JTAG and the TAP controller.
questions.st: AMD Dft Engineer Dallas Tx interview
questions.a: JTAG (IEEE 1149.1) is a serial test port with TCK, TMS, TDI, TDO and optional TRST. The TAP controller is a 16-state FSM driven by TMS on TCK edges; it selects whether TDI to TDO shifts through the instruction register or a data register (bypass, IDCODE, boundary scan or internal test registers), and has capture, shift and update phases. Boundary scan lets you test board interconnect without probes; the same port is used for debug, MBIST control and programming.

questions.q: Explain a branch predictor. How do ARM and x86 branch predictors differ?
questions.st: AMD Cpu Performance Modeling Engineer India interview
questions.a: A branch predictor guesses the direction and target of a branch so fetch can continue without waiting. Simple ones use 2-bit saturating counters indexed by the PC; better ones use global history (gshare), tournament predictors, or TAGE and perceptron-style predictors, plus a branch target buffer and a return-address stack. Arm and x86 cores use the same families of techniques; the differences are in the implementation details of each core (table sizes, history lengths, how variable-length x86 instructions are handled in fetch), not the ISA itself.

questions.q: Explain out-of-order processors and why instruction-level parallelism matters.
questions.st: AMD Cpu Design Verification Engineer Austin Tx interview
questions.a: An out-of-order processor executes instructions when their operands are ready, not strictly in program order. It renames registers to remove false dependencies, holds instructions in reservation stations or an issue queue, executes them on multiple units, and retires them in order from a reorder buffer. Instruction-level parallelism is the number of independent instructions available at once; exploiting it hides latencies (cache misses, long operations) and raises IPC without needing a higher clock.

questions.q: Explain overlapping and non-overlapping implication in assertions.
questions.st: AMD Design Verification Engineer United States interview
questions.a: In SVA, an implication a |-> b is overlapping: when a matches, b is checked in the same cycle in which a ended. a |=> b is non-overlapping: b is checked one cycle later, so it equals a |-> ##1 b. If the antecedent does not match, the property passes vacuously. Use |-> when the response is combinational, |=> when it comes on the next clock, and ##n for longer delays.

questions.q: Explain stuck-at, stuck-open and delay fault models.
questions.st: AMD Dft Engineer Dallas Tx interview
questions.a: Stuck-at faults model a node permanently at 0 or 1; they are the basis of most ATPG. Stuck-open faults model a transistor that never conducts; in CMOS this can make a gate keep its old value, so detection needs a two-pattern test (an initialisation vector then a test vector). Delay faults model a path or gate that is too slow: transition faults (slow-to-rise or slow-to-fall at a node) and path delay faults (accumulated delay on a path), tested at speed with launch-on-capture or launch-on-shift patterns.

questions.q: Explain the 4-phase and 2-phase handshakes.
questions.st: AMD Asic Design Engineer United States interview
questions.a: Both transfer data across clock domains with req and ack. In a 4-phase (return-to-zero) handshake: the sender raises req, the receiver takes the data and raises ack, the sender lowers req, and the receiver lowers ack, so each transfer needs four synchronised transitions. In a 2-phase (non-return-to-zero) handshake every toggle of req is a request and every toggle of ack an acknowledgement, so only two transitions per transfer: faster, but the logic must detect toggles (XOR with a delayed copy) instead of levels.

questions.q: Explain the VLSI design flow.
questions.st: AMD Validation Engineer New Delhi interview
questions.a: Specification and architecture, then RTL design in Verilog or VHDL, functional verification (simulation, formal, emulation), lint and CDC checks, then synthesis to a gate netlist with timing constraints, DFT insertion, and equivalence checking. Physical design follows: floorplanning, power planning, placement, clock tree synthesis, routing, then sign-off checks: static timing analysis across corners, IR drop and EM, DRC, LVS and antenna. After tape-out the GDSII is fabricated, and the chip goes through post-silicon validation and production test.

questions.q: Give an example of an asynchronous finite state machine.
questions.st: AMD Asic Design Engineer Intern Markham On interview
questions.a: An asynchronous FSM changes state on input changes without a clock; its state is held in feedback loops. The simplest example is an SR latch: S sets the state to 1, R resets it to 0, and the feedback holds it. Another is a C-element (Muller element), whose output goes high when all inputs are high and low when all are low, used in handshake circuits. Asynchronous FSMs need careful state assignment to avoid races and hazards, since only one state bit should change at a time.

questions.q: Given a black-box circuit and its truth table, use it to implement a NOT gate.
questions.st: AMD Design Verification Engineer Markham On interview
questions.a: Look at the truth table for a way to make the output the complement of one input. If the black box has an input that, when tied to a constant, makes the output follow the inverse of another input (for example a NAND with one input tied to 1, a NOR with one input tied to 0, a XOR with one input tied to 1, or a MUX selecting between constants), tie the other inputs to those constants or to the same signal and use the remaining input as A. Check every row: the output must be 1 when A is 0 and 0 when A is 1.

questions.q: Given a piece of code, is it a sequential or combinational circuit? If sequential, how many clock cycles does it take?
questions.st: AMD Gpu Verification Engineer Orlando Fl interview
questions.a: Check for storage and a clock. Code that uses always @(posedge clk) with non-blocking assignments, or any reg that keeps its value when not assigned (an incomplete if or case), describes sequential logic; code where every output is a function of the current inputs only (continuous assigns or always @(*) with every output assigned in every branch) is combinational. For sequential code, count the register stages between the input and the output: each posedge-clocked register adds one cycle of latency.

questions.q: How do you access a register and confirm whether it is 12 bits wide?
questions.st: AMD Asic Design Verification Engineer Bengaluru Karnataka interview
questions.a: Write a pattern with all bits set (for example all ones, or a walking 1 across the bit positions) to the register, then read it back. The bits that read back as 1 are implemented; a 12-bit register returns only the lower 12 bits set and the upper bits as 0 (or their reset value). Also check that writes to the unused upper bits have no effect and that the reset value matches the spec; a UVM RAL model can do this automatically with its bit-bash sequence.

questions.q: How would you verify a 32-bit, two-input ALU when 2^32 x 2^32 combinations are impossible to simulate?
questions.st: AMD Design Verification Internship United States interview
questions.a: You cannot simulate exhaustively, so verify smartly. Use constrained-random stimulus with a reference model in the scoreboard, and bias it toward corner values: 0, 1, all ones, the most negative and positive numbers, carry-propagation patterns and overflow boundaries. Do directed tests per operation, add assertions for flags (zero, carry, overflow), and close functional coverage on operations crossed with operand classes. Because an ALU is regular, verify a small-width version exhaustively and prove the full width with formal equivalence against a reference.

questions.q: Out of 100 driver versions, all versions after the first broken one are also broken. How do you find the first broken one quickly?
questions.st: AMD Systems Validation Toronto On interview
questions.a: Use binary search. Test version 50: if it is broken, the first broken version is in 1 to 50; otherwise it is in 51 to 100. Keep halving the range. Because every version after the first broken one is also broken, the property is monotonic, so binary search finds it in at most 7 tests (log2 100 rounded up), instead of up to 100 with a linear search. This is exactly what git bisect does.

questions.q: What are testability, observability and controllability?
questions.st: AMD Dft Engineer Dallas Tx interview
questions.a: Controllability is how easily a test can set a node to 0 or 1 from the primary inputs; observability is how easily the value of a node can be seen at a primary output. Testability combines both: a fault can only be detected if the faulty node can be controlled to the opposite value and its effect observed. Scan chains improve both by making every flip-flop directly loadable and readable, and test points can be inserted for hard-to-reach nodes.

questions.q: What are the three states of a tri-state buffer?
questions.st: AMD Hardware Engineer Toronto On interview
questions.a: A tri-state buffer has three output states: logic 0, logic 1, and high impedance (Z). When the enable is active, it drives its input value (0 or 1); when the enable is inactive, both output transistors are off and the output floats, so another driver can use the same wire. That is how shared buses work, with only one driver enabled at a time; two drivers enabled with opposite values cause contention.

questions.q: What are universal gates and why are they important?
questions.st: AMD interview experience for hardware profile

questions.q: What circuit does an if-else statement synthesize to?
questions.st: AMD Hardware Intern Bengaluru interview
questions.a: An if-else in a combinational always block synthesizes to a 2:1 multiplexer: the condition drives the select line and the two branches are the data inputs. Chains of if-else if give a priority multiplexer chain, with the first condition having the highest priority. Inside a clocked always block, the same mux feeds the D input of a flip-flop. If some branch leaves an output unassigned in combinational logic, synthesis infers a latch.

questions.q: What is BIST?
questions.st: AMD Dft Engineer Dallas Tx interview
questions.a: BIST (built-in self-test) puts the test hardware on the chip itself: a pattern generator (often an LFSR), a response compactor (a MISR or a comparator) and a controller. Logic BIST tests random logic through the scan chains; memory BIST (MBIST) runs march algorithms on embedded memories and compares the read data. BIST allows at-speed testing, reduces tester cost and pin needs, and can be run in the field for power-on self-test.

questions.q: What is a race condition?
questions.st: AMD Asic Design Engineer Toronto On interview
questions.a: A race condition is when the result depends on the order of events that happen at the same time. In Verilog it typically appears when several always blocks triggered by the same clock edge read and write the same variable with blocking assignments, so the simulator's arbitrary ordering decides the result; using non-blocking assignments for sequential logic avoids it. In hardware it is when two signals racing through different paths decide the outcome, for example in asynchronous logic.

questions.q: What is the checkpoint theorem?
questions.st: AMD Dft Engineer Dallas Tx interview
questions.a: The checkpoint theorem says that in a combinational circuit, a test set that detects all single stuck-at faults on the checkpoints also detects all single stuck-at faults in the circuit. Checkpoints are the primary inputs and the fanout branches. It reduces the number of faults the ATPG has to target, because faults on other lines are equivalent to or dominated by checkpoint faults.

questions.q: What is the difference between combinational and sequential logic?
questions.st: AMD Design Verification Engineer Canada interview
questions.a: Combinational logic produces outputs that depend only on the current inputs, with no memory: gates, multiplexers, adders, decoders. Sequential logic has memory: its outputs depend on current inputs and on stored state, held in latches or flip-flops, and it usually changes state on a clock edge: counters, registers, FSMs. In Verilog, combinational logic is written with assign or always @(*), sequential logic with always @(posedge clk).

questions.q: What is the difference between temporal and spatial locality?
questions.st: AMD Design Verification United States interview
questions.a: Temporal locality: an address that was accessed is likely to be accessed again soon (loop variables, a stack). Caches exploit it by keeping recently used data. Spatial locality: addresses near a recently accessed one are likely to be accessed soon (arrays, sequential instructions). Caches exploit it by fetching a whole line of several bytes and with hardware prefetching.

questions.q: Why do we need structural testing?
questions.st: AMD Dft Engineer Dallas Tx interview
questions.a: Functional tests check what the chip does, but for millions of gates they would need impossible numbers of patterns and still not prove that every node works. Structural testing targets the physical implementation: it uses fault models (stuck-at, transition) and scan to test each gate and net directly, with ATPG generating compact patterns and a measurable fault coverage. It catches manufacturing defects efficiently, regardless of how the logic is used.

questions.q: Why do we need testing, and what is a fault analysis system?
questions.st: AMD Dft Engineer Dallas Tx interview
questions.a: Manufacturing is not perfect: particles, shorts, opens and process variation create defective chips, so every die must be tested before shipping. Fault analysis uses fault models (stuck-at, transition, bridging) and fault simulation to measure how many possible defects a pattern set detects (fault coverage), and to generate tests with ATPG. In silicon failure analysis, the failing patterns are diagnosed to locate the physical defect.

questions.q: Explain the Tomasulo algorithm.
questions.st: AMD Design Verification Engineer Boxborough Ma interview
questions.a: Tomasulo's algorithm schedules instructions out of order in hardware. Instructions are issued in order to reservation stations attached to the functional units; registers are renamed by tagging each pending result with the reservation station that will produce it, which removes WAR and WAW hazards. An instruction waits in its station until all its operands are available, then executes; results are broadcast on a common data bus to every waiting station and the register file. Modern cores add a reorder buffer for in-order commit and precise exceptions.

questions.q: What is the D-algorithm?
questions.st: AMD Dft Engineer Dallas Tx interview
questions.a: The D-algorithm is a classic ATPG algorithm for stuck-at faults. It uses a five-value algebra: 0, 1, X, D (1 in the good circuit, 0 in the faulty one) and D-bar. It first activates the fault by setting the faulty line to D or D-bar, then propagates the D to a primary output by setting side inputs of gates on the path to non-controlling values (D-drive), and finally justifies all the required internal values back to primary inputs, backtracking on conflicts.

questions.q: Explain the UART, SPI, I2C and PCIe protocols.
questions.st: AMD interview experience for hardware profile
questions.a: UART is asynchronous serial: a start bit, 5 to 9 data bits, optional parity and stop bits, with both sides agreeing on the baud rate; no clock wire. SPI is synchronous full duplex with SCLK, MOSI, MISO and a chip select per slave, simple and fast. I2C is a two-wire bus (SCL, SDA, open drain with pull-ups) with 7-bit addresses, start and stop conditions, ACK bits, multiple masters and clock stretching. PCIe is a high-speed point-to-point serial link with lanes, packetised transactions in transaction, data-link and physical layers, credits and link training.

questions.q: From a timing diagram, calculate the minimum and maximum delay.
questions.st: AMD Asic Design Engineer Intern Markham On interview
questions.a: Trace each path from the changing input to the output. The minimum delay is the time from the input edge to the first change at the output (the fastest path and the contamination delays); the maximum delay is the time until the output finally settles (the slowest path and the propagation delays). Write each as a sum of gate delays along the path, and remember that glitches can appear between the two.

questions.q: A UVM environment has 3 agents on separate interfaces. Wrong stimulus on agent1 raises an error pin on interface3, which agent2's monitor sees; agent2 must then perform a read. How do you make sure agent2 drives a read for every such error?
questions.st: AMD Verification Engineer Bengaluru interview
questions.a: Make the response event driven rather than relying on timing. Agent2's monitor sees the error pin and writes a transaction to an analysis port; a virtual sequencer, or agent2's sequence, subscribes through an analysis FIFO and, for every error item received, starts a read sequence on agent2's sequencer. Use a blocking get on the FIFO so no error is missed even when errors come back to back, and check in the scoreboard that the number of reads equals the number of injected errors.

questions.q: A chip does add, subtract, multiply and divide on 8-bit values, keeps up to 20 operands on a stack, and has error bits for arithmetic overflow and stack overflow. What corner cases and errors would you test, and how would you write those tests in a Verilog testbench?
questions.st: AMD Design Verification Engineer Markham On interview
questions.a: Corner cases: operations on 0, 1, 127, -128 and 255; results that overflow 8 bits on add, subtract and multiply; division by zero and division results that round; pushing the 20th and 21st operand (stack full and stack overflow); popping or computing with an empty or nearly empty stack; reset in the middle of an operation; back-to-back operations; and checking that the error bits set, stay set as specified and clear correctly. In a Verilog testbench, use tasks for push and operate, a reference model to compute expected results and flags, directed tests for each corner, random sequences, and a self-check that prints PASS or FAIL.

questions.q: Describe a UVM testbench and explain how sequences and drivers are connected.
questions.st: AMD Design Verification Engineer Boxborough Ma interview
questions.a: A UVM testbench has a test that builds an environment; the environment contains agents (each with a sequencer, driver and monitor), a scoreboard and coverage collectors, and gets the virtual interface from config_db. Sequences generate sequence items on a sequencer. The driver has a seq_item_port connected to the sequencer's seq_item_export in the agent's connect_phase; the driver calls get_next_item(), drives the item onto the interface pins, then item_done(). Monitors publish observed transactions through analysis ports.

questions.q: Explain how OOP concepts are used in UVM.
questions.st: AMD Senior Verification Engineer Bengaluru interview
questions.a: UVM is built on SystemVerilog classes. Encapsulation: each component (driver, monitor, scoreboard) holds its own data and methods. Inheritance: you extend base classes such as uvm_driver or uvm_sequence_item and override methods like run_phase. Polymorphism: a handle of a base type can point to a derived object, and with virtual methods plus the factory you can swap in derived components or sequences (type and instance overrides) without editing the environment. Parameterised classes give typed ports and sequencers.

questions.q: For an 8-bit stack-based chip, list the corner cases and possible errors, and how you would test them in a Verilog testbench.
questions.st: AMD Design Verification Engineer interview, Markham
questions.a: Corner cases: operand values 0, 1, max positive, max negative and 255; add and multiply overflow; subtract underflow; divide by zero; the stack at 0, 1, 19, 20 and 21 entries (empty, full and overflow); popping an empty stack; reset during an operation; back-to-back commands. Possible errors: wrong overflow flags, flags not clearing, a lost or duplicated operand at the stack boundary. Write tasks for each command, a reference model in the testbench, directed tests per corner, a random test, and compare results and flags after every operation.

questions.q: What are the main differences between the UVM monitor and driver classes?
questions.st: AMD Verification Engineer Boxborough Ma interview
questions.a: The driver converts sequence items into pin activity: it pulls items from the sequencer with get_next_item() and item_done() and drives the interface, so it is active. The monitor only observes: it samples the interface, rebuilds transactions and broadcasts them on an analysis port to scoreboards and coverage, and it never drives signals. A passive agent has only a monitor; the driver is tied to the protocol's timing, while the monitor must be correct even when another component drives.

questions.q: What mechanism connects the UVM driver and the sequencer?
questions.st: AMD Verification Engineer Sunnyvale Ca interview
questions.a: TLM ports. The driver's seq_item_port (a uvm_seq_item_pull_port) is connected to the sequencer's seq_item_export in the agent's connect_phase. The driver calls get_next_item() (blocking) or try_next_item(), drives the item, then calls item_done(), optionally returning a response with put_response(). Sequences run on the sequencer with start_item() and finish_item(), and the sequencer arbitrates between sequences.

questions.q: What types of assertions are there in SystemVerilog?
questions.st: AMD Design Verification United States interview
questions.a: Immediate assertions (assert (cond) else ...) are checked like an if statement in procedural code at the time they execute; deferred immediate assertions (assert #0 or assert final) avoid glitches. Concurrent assertions (assert property) are evaluated on a clock, can describe sequences over time, and run in parallel with the design. Alongside assert, there are assume (constraints for formal) and cover (check a scenario happens) statements.

questions.q: Write a UVM driver for APB that supports outstanding transactions.
questions.st: AMD Design Verification Engineer Vietnam interview
questions.a: Use a pipelined driver: one thread drives the address phase and another collects responses, connected by a queue. The address thread gets an item with get_next_item(), drives PADDR, PWRITE and PSEL for the setup phase, then PENABLE for the access phase, pushes the item into a pending queue and calls item_done() without waiting for PREADY. The response thread waits for PREADY on the next pending item, captures PRDATA and PSLVERR and sends the response with put_response(). Note that APB itself allows only one transfer in progress; outstanding support really means the driver can accept new items while the bus completes the previous one.

questions.q: How do Verilog simulators differ from C++ simulators?
questions.st: AMD Hardware Engineer United States interview
questions.a: A Verilog simulator models hardware: an event-driven scheduler with simulation time, concurrency (many always blocks running in parallel), 4-state values (0, 1, X, Z), and delays, and it executes RTL or gates. A C++ simulator (like Verilator, or a C++ architecture model) compiles the design into a sequential program, usually 2-state and cycle-based without delays, so it runs much faster but cannot model X propagation or timing. C++ models are used for performance and architecture exploration.

questions.q: What are the types of modelling in Verilog?
questions.st: AMD interview experience for hardware profile
questions.a: Verilog supports several modelling styles. Gate level (structural with primitives such as and, or and nand), switch level (nmos, pmos), dataflow (continuous assign statements with operators) and behavioural (always and initial blocks with if, case and loops). Structural modelling instantiates and connects modules. Real designs mix behavioural RTL for logic with structural connection at the top level.

questions.q: Which Verilog constructs are synthesizable and which are not?
questions.st: AMD Verification Engineer Sunnyvale Ca interview
questions.a: Synthesizable: module structure, assign, always @(posedge clk) and always @(*), if, case, for loops with fixed bounds, operators, parameters, generate, functions, and tasks without timing. Not synthesizable (or ignored): initial blocks (except for FPGA initial values), delays (#10), $display, $random and other system tasks, wait and event controls with arbitrary timing, force/release, fork-join, real numbers, file I/O and dynamic loops. Testbenches use these freely.

questions.q: Why use architecture simulators instead of simulating workloads in RTL?
questions.st: AMD Cpu Performance Modeling Engineer India interview
questions.a: RTL simulation runs at a few hundred to a few thousand cycles per second for a full CPU, so running real workloads (billions of instructions) is impossible, and the RTL does not exist yet when architecture decisions are made. Architecture simulators (gem5, C++ performance models) are cycle-approximate but thousands of times faster, easy to change, and let you explore cache sizes, predictors or core width before writing RTL. RTL is used later to confirm correctness and timing.

questions.q: Design a NAND gate in CMOS.
questions.st: Analog Devices Dft Engineer Bhubaneshwar Odisha interview
questions.a: A CMOS NAND2 uses two PMOS transistors in parallel between VDD and the output, and two NMOS transistors in series between the output and ground, with input A on one PMOS/NMOS pair and B on the other. If either input is 0, one PMOS turns on and pulls the output high, while the series NMOS path is broken. Only when both inputs are 1 do both NMOS conduct and pull the output low while both PMOS are off. The series NMOS are usually sized about twice as wide to match pull-down strength.

questions.q: What are the non-idealities of MOS capacitance?
questions.st: Analog Devices Senior Engineer Modeling And Verification India interview
questions.a: MOS capacitances are not fixed: the gate capacitance changes with the operating region (accumulation, depletion, inversion; Cgs and Cgd split differently in cut-off, linear and saturation). There are overlap capacitances (Cgso, Cgdo) causing the Miller effect, and junction capacitances (Cdb, Csb) that depend on the reverse bias voltage. Gate leakage through thin oxides, poly depletion and quantum effects reduce the effective capacitance, and fringing fields add to it. All of these make delays voltage dependent.

questions.q: What is a TVS diode?
questions.st: Analog Devices Entry Level Associate Product Applications Engineer Chandler Arizona interview
questions.a: A TVS (transient voltage suppressor) diode protects circuits from voltage spikes such as ESD, inductive kickback and surges. It is placed in parallel with the line; in normal operation it is off (reverse biased below its standoff voltage), and when a spike exceeds its breakdown voltage it conducts very quickly and clamps the voltage, diverting the surge current to ground. Key specs are standoff voltage, clamping voltage, peak pulse current and capacitance.

questions.q: A current source drives a switch in series with a capacitor that has another switch across it. Describe the voltage response as each switch closes.
questions.st: Analog Devices Mixed Signal Verification Engineer Valencia Valencian Community interview
questions.a: With the capacitor's shorting switch closed, the current source's current flows through the switch and the capacitor voltage stays at 0. When that switch opens (and the series switch is closed), the constant current charges the capacitor linearly: V = I t / C, a ramp. When the series switch opens, the current stops and the capacitor holds its voltage. Closing the shorting switch again discharges it to 0. Repeating this produces a sawtooth.

questions.q: Compare buck, boost and linear regulators.

A buck converter switches an inductor to step the voltage down with high efficiency (often over 90%), at the cost of switching noise and ripple. A boost converter uses the inductor to step the voltage up. Choose linear for low noise and small drops, switching for efficiency or large ratios.

When it discharges through R, v(t) = V e^(-t/RC), falling to 37% after one RC. The current reverses direction during discharge.

questions.q: Explain channel-length modulation.
questions.st: Analog Devices Senior Engineer Modeling And Verification India interview
questions.a: In saturation, a larger drain voltage widens the depletion region at the drain end, so the pinch-off point moves toward the source and the effective channel length shrinks. The drain current therefore still rises slightly with VDS: ID = (k/2)(VGS - Vt)^2 (1 + lambda VDS), where lambda is the channel-length modulation parameter. It gives the transistor a finite output resistance ro = 1/(lambda ID), which limits amplifier gain, and it is stronger in short-channel devices.

questions.q: Explain the body effect.
questions.st: Analog Devices Senior Engineer Modeling And Verification India interview
questions.a: The threshold voltage of a MOSFET depends on the source-to-body voltage. When the source is above the body (a positive VSB for an NMOS), the depletion region under the channel widens, more charge is needed to invert the channel, and Vt increases: Vt = Vt0 + gamma (sqrt(2phiF + VSB) - sqrt(2phiF)). It slows transistors stacked in series, such as the upper NMOS in a NAND, and reduces the gain of source followers.

For each state bit, derive the next-state equation from the table, simplify it with K-maps (for D flip-flops the D input equals the next state), and derive the output equations: from the state only for Moore, from state and inputs for Mealy. Finally draw the flip-flops with the combinational logic.

questions.q: How does increasing the order of a low-pass filter change its Bode plot, and what does the circuit look like?
questions.st: Analog Devices Hardware Engineer Israel interview
questions.a: Each order adds a pole, so the roll-off above the cut-off gets steeper: -20 dB per decade for first order, -40 dB for second, and -20n dB per decade for order n, and the phase shift grows to -90n degrees. The circuit cascades RC sections or, better, uses active stages such as Sallen-Key or multiple-feedback op-amp filters (two poles per stage), or an LC ladder. Higher order gives a sharper transition but more components and possible peaking depending on the Q.

questions.q: How would you implement a sine function in hardware?
questions.st: Analog Devices Hardware Engineer Wilmington Massachusetts interview
questions.a: Options: a lookup table in ROM holding a quarter wave (using symmetry for the other quadrants), with linear interpolation between entries for more precision; the CORDIC algorithm, which computes sine and cosine with only shifts, adds and a small angle table, one bit of accuracy per iteration; or a polynomial approximation (Taylor or minimax) evaluated with multipliers. The choice trades memory, latency and precision.

questions.q: Identify the logic function a given network of gates implements.
questions.st: Analog Devices Hardware Engineering Co Op Switzerland interview
questions.a: Work from the inputs to the output: write the Boolean expression at each gate output, then substitute through the network to get a single expression, and simplify it with Boolean algebra or a K-map. Alternatively, build the truth table by trying all input combinations. Recognise common patterns: a NAND of NANDs is an OR of products, and XOR appears as a b' + a' b.

questions.q: Is a given RC circuit a low-pass or a high-pass filter?
questions.st: Analog Devices Hardware Intern Limerick County Limerick interview
questions.a: Look at what happens at low and high frequencies, treating the capacitor as open at DC and short at high frequency. If the output is taken across the capacitor (series R, then C to ground), high frequencies are shorted to ground, so it is a low-pass filter. If the output is taken across the resistor (series C, then R to ground), DC is blocked and high frequencies pass, so it is a high-pass filter. Either way the cut-off is f = 1/(2 pi R C).

questions.q: What is a critical path?
questions.st: Analog Devices Design Verification Engineer Raleigh North Carolina interview
questions.a: The critical path is the longest-delay path between two sequential elements (or from input to output) in a design. It sets the maximum clock frequency: the clock period must be at least the clock-to-Q delay plus the critical path's combinational delay plus the setup time (minus useful skew). Timing optimisation targets it with faster cells, logic restructuring, pipelining or retiming.

questions.q: What is the best way to protect an amplifier input from overvoltage?
questions.st: Analog Devices Verification Engineer Limerick County Limerick interview
questions.a: Limit the current and clamp the voltage. Put a series resistor in the input to limit the current, and clamp diodes (Schottky, low leakage) from the input to the supply rails so the voltage cannot exceed the rails by more than a diode drop; for larger events add a TVS diode at the connector. Make sure the supplies can absorb the clamped current, and pick a resistor that does not hurt noise or bandwidth. Some amplifiers have internal protection with a specified maximum current.

questions.st: Analog Devices Hardware Engineer Bengaluru Karnataka interview
questions.a: Static timing analysis checks that every timing path in a design meets setup and hold without simulation vectors. It breaks the design into paths from start points (inputs, clock pins of flops) to end points (data pins, outputs), computes arrival times using cell and wire delays, and compares them with required times from the clock constraints (period, uncertainty, latency). It is exhaustive and fast, but it relies on correct constraints for false and multicycle paths, and runs across corners and modes.

questions.q: An interconnect has 3 AHB masters and 1 APB master on one side and 3 APB slaves on the other, with given address ranges; some masters get error responses for the top range. Write the top-level testbench and the coverpoints and bins you would use.
questions.st: Analog Devices Design Verification Engineer India interview
questions.a: Build an environment with three AHB master agents and one APB master agent (active), three APB slave agents (reactive responders or memory models), a scoreboard with an address map that predicts which slave each access reaches and which accesses must get an error response, and a virtual sequencer to coordinate traffic. Coverpoints: master id, slave reached (bins per address range), read or write, error versus okay, burst type, crossed master by slave by response so the error-only combinations (masters 3 and APB to the top range) and the allowed ones (masters 1 and 2) are both hit, plus concurrent access from several masters.

questions.q: Explain virtual functions and polymorphism in SystemVerilog.
questions.st: Analog Devices Design Verification Engineer Raleigh North Carolina interview
questions.a: A virtual method is resolved at run time by the object's type, not the handle's type. If a base class declares virtual function display() and a derived class overrides it, calling display() through a base-class handle that points to a derived object runs the derived version. This is polymorphism: generic code (a scoreboard, a driver, the UVM factory) works with base handles while the behaviour comes from the derived classes. Without virtual, the base version always runs.

questions.q: What are full_case and parallel_case in Verilog?
questions.st: Analog Devices Design Verification Intern Mangalore Karnataka interview
questions.a: They are synthesis directives on a case statement. full_case tells synthesis that all possible case values are covered, so it should not infer a latch for missing items; parallel_case says the items are mutually exclusive, so no priority logic is needed. Both change the synthesized logic without changing simulation, which can cause a simulation-synthesis mismatch. Prefer a default branch and unique or priority case in SystemVerilog, which also check the assumption in simulation.

questions.q: What is X in Verilog?
questions.st: Analog Devices Design Verification Intern Mangalore Karnataka interview
questions.a: X is the unknown value in Verilog's 4-state logic (0, 1, X, Z). It appears for uninitialised registers, multiple drivers with conflicting values, out-of-range selects, or operations involving X. Simulation propagates X pessimistically or optimistically depending on the construct (an if (x) takes the else branch, which can hide bugs). X is useful to find missing resets; synthesis treats assignments of X as don't-care.

questions.q: What is a synthesis-simulation mismatch?
questions.st: Analog Devices Design Verification Intern Mangalore Karnataka interview
questions.a: It is when the synthesized netlist behaves differently from the RTL simulation. Common causes: incomplete sensitivity lists (simulation does not update while hardware does), full_case and parallel_case pragmas, X optimism in if or case statements, initial blocks and delays that synthesis ignores, blocking assignments used in sequential logic, and latches inferred where combinational logic was intended. Gate-level simulation and equivalence checking catch these.

questions.q: How do you safely transfer a signal across clock domains? What are the risks if it is not handled correctly?
questions.st: Apple Hardware Engineer interview, Cupertino
questions.a: For a single bit, pass it through a two-flop (or three-flop) synchronizer in the destination clock domain; metastability can still occur in the first flop, but it has a full cycle to resolve. Fast pulses must be stretched or converted to a toggle first. For multi-bit data, use a handshake with a synchronised request and acknowledge, an asynchronous FIFO with Gray-coded pointers, or a mux-recirculation scheme. If not handled, you get metastability, random wrong values, data incoherence where bits are sampled in different cycles, and lost pulses, causing intermittent failures in silicon.

questions.q: How is MBIST triggered when scan mode is low during BIST?
questions.st: Apple Soc Dft Engineer interview
questions.a: MBIST is usually started through a separate control path, not functional scan mode. A JTAG TAP instruction or an IJTAG (IEEE 1687) network writes the MBIST controller's control registers (start, algorithm, memory select) through test data registers, or a dedicated BIST enable or test-mode pin starts it. The controller then runs the march algorithm on the memories at functional speed and sets done and pass/fail bits that are read back through JTAG. Scan enable is held low because the logic is in functional, at-speed mode during the run.

questions.q: What problems come from mixing positive- and negative-edge flops in scan?
questions.st: Apple Soc Dft Engineer interview
questions.a: If a positive-edge flop follows a negative-edge flop in the same chain, data can shift through both on one clock cycle and patterns break; mixing edges also creates half-cycle timing paths that are hard to close at shift speed. The usual fix is to order the chain with all negative-edge flops first, followed by the positive-edge flops, so data shifts correctly, or to put a lockup latch between domains. It also complicates capture and at-speed test.

questions.q: Describe how the FFT and inverse FFT work.
questions.st: Apple Silicon Validation Engineer interview
questions.a: The discrete Fourier transform converts N time samples into N frequency components; computing it directly needs N^2 multiplications. The FFT (for example radix-2 Cooley-Tukey) splits the DFT recursively into DFTs of even and odd samples and combines them with butterfly operations using twiddle factors, reducing the work to about N log2 N. The inverse FFT is the same algorithm with conjugated twiddle factors and a 1/N scaling, taking a spectrum back to time samples.

questions.q: Design a sawtooth generator from a square pulse and a constant current, and derive the integrator circuit.
questions.st: Apple Hardware Systems Integration Engineer Sunnyvale California interview
questions.a: Charge a capacitor with a constant current: V = I t / C rises linearly, giving the ramp of the sawtooth. Use the square pulse to drive a switch (a transistor) across the capacitor that discharges it quickly at the start of each period, so the voltage resets to 0 and the ramp starts again. An op-amp integrator gives the same result with a precise ground reference: input current into the virtual ground charges the feedback capacitor, Vout = -(1/RC) integral of Vin dt, with a reset switch across the capacitor.

questions.q: Design an RC filter with gain.
questions.st: Apple Battery Hardware Engineer Houston Texas interview
questions.a: Use an op-amp. For a low-pass filter with gain, make an inverting amplifier with Rin at the input and Rf in parallel with Cf in the feedback: DC gain = -Rf/Rin and cut-off f = 1/(2 pi Rf Cf). Or put a passive RC low-pass in front of a non-inverting amplifier with gain 1 + Rf/Rg. For a high-pass filter, put a capacitor in series with Rin instead.

questions.q: Explain polymorphism in C++. Which base-class members can a child class not inherit?
questions.st: Apple Emulation Engineer Santa Clara California interview
questions.a: Polymorphism lets one interface have many implementations: with virtual functions, a call through a base-class pointer or reference runs the derived class's override, decided at run time through the vtable. Compile-time polymorphism comes from function overloading and templates. A derived class does not inherit constructors (unless with using), the destructor, the copy assignment operator, or friends; private members are inherited but not accessible.

questions.q: How do the different ADC architectures compare in speed?
questions.st: Apple Analog And Mixed Signal Engineer Irvine California interview
questions.a: From fastest to slowest: flash ADCs (one comparator per level, a single cycle, GHz rates but 2^N comparators, so low resolution); pipelined ADCs (several stages, high throughput with latency, tens to hundreds of MSPS at 10 to 14 bits); SAR ADCs (binary search, N cycles per conversion, moderate speed and very low power, up to about 18 bits); and sigma-delta ADCs (oversampling and noise shaping, slow but 16 to 24 bits, used for audio and precision measurement).

questions.q: How does a current mirror work?
questions.st: Apple Hardware Engineer Intern interview
questions.a: A current mirror copies a reference current. A diode-connected transistor M1 (gate tied to drain) carries the reference current Iref, which sets its VGS; a second transistor M2 shares the same gate-source voltage, so in saturation it conducts Iout = Iref (W/L)2 / (W/L)1. Errors come from channel-length modulation (the two VDS values differ), mismatch, and the output resistance; cascode or Wilson mirrors raise the output resistance and accuracy.

questions.q: How would you tell whether latency or bandwidth is the bottleneck?
questions.st: Apple Gpu Performance Modeling Engineer Cupertino California interview
questions.a: Measure how the time changes as you vary each one. If performance improves with more outstanding requests (more parallelism) and achieved bandwidth is far below peak, the workload is latency-bound; if achieved bandwidth is near the peak and adding parallelism does not help, it is bandwidth-bound. Use counters for memory throughput, queue occupancy and stall reasons, apply Little's law (in-flight requests = bandwidth x latency), and compare the arithmetic intensity against the roofline.

questions.q: What are the main challenges in implementing an out-of-order execution engine, and how do you ensure correctness?
questions.st: Apple Hardware Engineer interview, Cupertino
questions.a: The challenges are tracking dependencies through register renaming, scheduling ready instructions every cycle with wakeup and select logic, handling memory ordering (load-store queues, store-to-load forwarding and memory disambiguation), recovering from branch mispredicts and exceptions, and doing all this within timing and power limits. Correctness comes from in-order commit through a reorder buffer, so architectural state updates only at retirement, which gives precise exceptions and lets speculative work be discarded. It is verified against an ISA reference model by comparing retired instructions.

questions.q: What is a TAP controller and how does it work?
questions.st: Apple Soc Dft Engineer interview
questions.a: The TAP (test access port) controller is a 16-state FSM in the JTAG standard, clocked by TCK and steered by the TMS pin. Its two main branches select either the instruction register path or the data register path, each with Capture, Shift, Exit, Pause and Update states. TMS held high for five clocks always returns it to Test-Logic-Reset. Instructions loaded through the IR select which data register (bypass, IDCODE, boundary scan or user registers) sits between TDI and TDO.

questions.q: What is an OCC (on-chip clock controller) used for?
questions.st: Apple Soc Dft Engineer interview
questions.a: An on-chip clock controller generates test clocks for scan. During shift it passes the slow tester clock; during capture it lets a programmable number of fast pulses from the functional PLL through, so at-speed transition tests can launch and capture at the real frequency. It also makes the clock switch-over glitch-free and is configured through scan or JTAG bits. Without it, the tester could not provide GHz capture clocks.

questions.q: What is register renaming? How does it work?
questions.st: Apple Design Verification Intern interview
questions.a: Register renaming maps the few architectural registers onto a larger pool of physical registers. Each instruction that writes a register gets a new free physical register, and a rename table maps later readers to the latest one. This removes false dependencies (WAR and WAW), so independent instructions using the same architectural register can execute out of order in parallel. Physical registers are freed when a later instruction that overwrites the same architectural register commits.

questions.q: Where should you place the decoupling capacitor on a power pin?
questions.st: Apple Hardware Engineer Sunnyvale California interview
questions.a: As close as possible to the power pin, with the shortest, widest connection to the pin and to the ground plane, ideally on the same side of the board with vias placed right next to the pads. Small-value (for example 100 nF) capacitors go nearest the pin to handle high-frequency current, with larger bulk capacitors farther away. The goal is minimum loop inductance between the capacitor and the chip's supply and ground pins.

questions.q: How do you calculate the theoretical maximum FLOPS of an architecture? Explain the roofline model.
questions.st: Apple Gpu Performance Modeling Engineer Cupertino California interview
questions.a: Peak FLOPS = number of cores x clock frequency x FLOPs per cycle per core (number of FMA units x SIMD lanes x 2, because an FMA counts as two operations). The roofline model plots attainable performance against arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte moved from memory): performance is the minimum of the peak compute (a flat roof) and memory bandwidth x intensity (a sloped roof). The kernel's intensity shows whether it is memory-bound (left of the ridge point) or compute-bound (right).

Instantiate it once in the top module and pass it to both blocks, or to the testbench through a virtual interface.

questions.q: How do formal and functional verification differ?
questions.st: Apple Formal Verification Engineer Cupertino California interview
questions.a: Functional (simulation-based) verification applies stimulus and checks the responses, so it only covers the scenarios that were simulated and relies on coverage to measure completeness. Formal verification uses mathematical proof: a tool explores every reachable state for all inputs and either proves that a property always holds or gives a counter-example trace. Formal is exhaustive but limited in design size and depth; simulation scales to full chips. They are used together.

questions.q: What would you use a SystemVerilog modport for?
questions.st: Apple Design Verification Intern interview (45 min)
questions.a: A modport defines the direction of each interface signal from the point of view of one user. For a bus interface you might have modport master (output req, addr; input gnt) and modport slave (input req, addr; output gnt). Connecting a module through a modport enforces those directions at compile time, documents the protocol roles, and can limit which tasks and functions each side may call.

questions.q: Find the depletion depth of a source/drain junction at 1e18/cm3 doping with a 0.72 V built-in potential.
questions.st: ARM interview questions (MOSFET, CMOS) 2021
questions.a: Use the one-sided step junction approximation: W = sqrt(2 eps_si Vbi / (q N)). With eps_si = 11.7 x 8.85e-14 = 1.04e-12 F/cm, Vbi = 0.72 V, q = 1.6e-19 C and N = 1e18 /cm3: W = sqrt(2 x 1.04e-12 x 0.72 / (1.6e-19 x 1e18)) = sqrt(9.4e-12) = about 3.1e-6 cm, so roughly 31 nm at zero bias. Reverse bias adds to Vbi and widens it.

questions.q: How can a depletion-mode NMOS be turned off?
questions.st: ARM interview questions (MOSFET, CMOS) 2021
questions.a: A depletion-mode NMOS conducts at VGS = 0 because its threshold voltage is negative. To turn it off, drive the gate below the source by more than |Vt|, that is VGS < Vt (a negative gate-source voltage). You can also make VSB positive to increase the threshold through the body effect.

questions.q: What is CMOS, and why are NMOS and PMOS used together?
questions.st: Arm Hardware Engineer Bengaluru Karnataka interview
questions.a: CMOS (complementary MOS) builds each gate from a PMOS pull-up network to VDD and an NMOS pull-down network to ground that are logical complements, so for any input exactly one network conducts. NMOS passes a strong 0 and PMOS a strong 1, so together the output swings fully rail to rail. In steady state there is no path from VDD to ground, so static power is almost zero (only leakage). That full swing, high noise margin and low power are why CMOS dominates digital logic.

questions.q: Design the memory and FPGA interface for a camera, given its frequency requirements.
questions.st: Arm Staff Hardware Engineer Turkey interview
questions.a: Start from the camera's data rate: pixel clock x bits per pixel, for example 1920 x 1080 x 30 fps x 16 bits = about 1 Gbit/s. Capture the camera bus (parallel DVP or MIPI CSI-2 lanes) in the camera's clock domain, cross into the system clock with an asynchronous FIFO sized for line bursts, then write frames to external DRAM through a DMA or AXI master with burst writes and double (ping-pong) buffering, so one frame is read while the next is written. Check that memory bandwidth covers both write and read traffic with margin, and add line buffers if processing needs neighbouring rows.

questions.q: Explain how caches and pipelines work.
questions.st: Arm Verification Engineer Cambridge Cambridgeshire interview
questions.a: A pipeline splits instruction execution into stages (fetch, decode, execute, memory, write-back) so several instructions are in flight at once and throughput approaches one instruction per cycle; hazards are handled by forwarding, stalls and branch prediction. A cache is a small fast memory near the core that holds recently used lines; on a hit data returns in a few cycles, on a miss the line is fetched from the next level. Caches keep the memory stage of the pipeline from stalling on slow DRAM.

questions.q: Explain how caches, the MMU and virtual memory work together.
questions.st: Arm Hardware Engineer Antibes Provence Alpes Cote Dazur interview
questions.a: The program uses virtual addresses. On each access the MMU looks up the TLB to translate the virtual page number to a physical frame number; on a TLB miss it walks the page tables in memory (often through the caches) and fills the TLB, checking permissions on the way. The physical address (or, in a VIPT L1, the virtual index plus the physical tag) then looks up the caches. Virtual memory provides isolation and paging to disk; the TLB and caches make the translation and data access fast.

questions.q: Explain pipeline stalls, the forwarding unit and the hazard detection unit in a RISC-V pipeline.
questions.st: Arm Graduate Hardware And Verification Engineer Italy interview
questions.a: A stall freezes the earlier stages and inserts a bubble when an instruction cannot proceed. The forwarding unit compares the source registers of the instruction in EX with the destination registers of instructions in MEM and WB, and muxes their results straight into the ALU inputs, so most RAW hazards need no stall. The hazard detection unit in ID catches the case forwarding cannot fix, a load followed by an instruction that uses its result: it stalls the PC and the IF/ID register for one cycle and turns the ID/EX control into a bubble.

questions.q: Explain the types of hazards in a CPU pipeline.
questions.st: Arm Graduate Hardware Engineer Cambridge Cambridgeshire interview
questions.a: Structural hazards: two instructions need the same hardware in the same cycle (for example one memory port for instructions and data). Data hazards: an instruction depends on a result not yet available (RAW, plus WAR and WAW in out-of-order machines). Control hazards: the next instruction address is unknown until a branch resolves. They are handled with extra resources, forwarding, stalls, register renaming, and branch prediction with flushing.

questions.q: How are instructions executed in a non-pipelined architecture versus a pipelined one?
questions.st: ARM interview experience for verification engineer intern (on-campus, virtual)
questions.a: In a non-pipelined (single-cycle or multi-cycle) design, one instruction goes through all steps before the next starts, so the time per instruction is the sum of all stage delays. In a pipelined design, each stage works on a different instruction every cycle; a single instruction still takes about the same total latency (slightly more because of pipeline registers), but a new instruction completes every cycle, so throughput rises by up to the number of stages, minus hazard stalls.

questions.q: How does a cache fetch data from main memory?
questions.st: Arm Cpu Verification New York New York interview
questions.a: On a miss, the cache controller allocates a line (choosing a victim with the replacement policy and writing it back if it is dirty), then sends a read request for the whole line, aligned to the line size, to the next level or the memory controller. The data comes back in bursts, often critical word first so the waiting load can continue early; the line is written into the data array, the tag and valid bit are updated, and the pending requests in the MSHR are completed.

questions.q: What are L1 and L2 caches, and how do they differ?
questions.st: ARM interview experience for verification engineer intern (on-campus, virtual)
questions.a: L1 is the smallest and fastest cache, closest to the core (typically 32 to 64 KB, a few cycles of latency), usually split into separate instruction and data caches. L2 is larger (hundreds of KB to a few MB) and slower (around 10 to 15 cycles), usually unified, and catches L1 misses. L1 is optimised for hit time, L2 for hit rate; they can be inclusive or exclusive of each other, and an L3 shared by all cores often sits beyond them.

questions.q: What are the hazards in a pipelined processor and how are they resolved?
questions.st: Arm Cpu Verification New York New York interview
questions.a: Structural hazards are resolved by duplicating resources (separate instruction and data memories) or stalling. Data hazards are resolved by forwarding results from later stages, stalling for load-use, and in out-of-order cores by register renaming and reservation stations. Control hazards are resolved by branch prediction, resolving branches early, delay slots in older ISAs, and flushing the wrong-path instructions on a misprediction.

questions.q: What is CPU pipelining, and what problems does it bring?
questions.st: Arm Hardware Engineer United Kingdom interview
questions.a: Pipelining overlaps the stages of consecutive instructions, like an assembly line, so one instruction can complete per cycle and the clock can be faster because each stage is short. The problems: hazards (structural, data, control) that cause stalls and need forwarding and prediction logic; branch mispredict penalties that grow with depth; extra pipeline-register area, power and latency; and more complex exception handling and verification.

questions.q: What is pipelining, and why does it matter in an SoC?
questions.st: Arm Hardware Engineer Intern Cambridge Cambridgeshire interview
questions.a: Pipelining splits a long operation into stages separated by registers so that several data items or instructions are processed at once. In an SoC it is used everywhere: CPU pipelines, DSP and video datapaths, bus interconnects and memory controllers. It raises the achievable clock frequency (shorter combinational paths) and throughput, at the cost of latency and area, and it is the main tool for closing timing on long paths.

questions.q: What is pipelining? What is cache coherency?
questions.st: Arm Design Verification Engineer United States interview

questions.q: What is the cache hierarchy?
questions.st: ARM interview experience for verification engineer intern (on-campus, virtual)
questions.a: Small, fast caches sit close to the core and larger, slower ones further away: L1 instruction and data caches per core, an L2 per core or cluster, and a shared last-level cache (L3 or system cache), then DRAM. Each level filters misses from the one above. The policies (inclusive or exclusive, write-back, coherence between cores) are chosen to balance hit latency, hit rate, area and power.

questions.q: What is the memory hierarchy?
questions.st: ARM interview experience for verification engineer intern (on-campus, virtual)
questions.a: Storage arranged from fastest, smallest and most expensive per bit to slowest, largest and cheapest: registers, L1, L2 and L3 caches (SRAM), main memory (DRAM), then flash or SSD and disk. Locality means most accesses hit the upper levels, so the system appears to have the speed of the top and the capacity of the bottom.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the memory management unit?
questions.st: Arm Graduate Cpu Engineer Antibes Provence Alpes Cote Dazur interview
questions.a: The MMU translates virtual addresses to physical addresses using page tables, with a TLB to cache translations. It enforces protection (read, write, execute and user or kernel permissions) so processes cannot touch each other's memory, raises page faults so the OS can load pages on demand, and sets memory attributes such as cacheable or device memory. It enables virtual memory, process isolation and shared libraries.

questions.q: What is virtual memory, and what are the ways to implement it?
questions.st: ARM interview experience for verification engineer intern (on-campus, virtual)
questions.a: Virtual memory gives each process its own address space that is mapped onto physical memory and backed by disk. It is implemented mostly with paging: memory is divided into fixed-size pages, page tables (often multi-level, or inverted or hashed) map virtual pages to physical frames, and a TLB caches the mappings. Segmentation, which maps variable-size segments with base and limit registers, is the older alternative, sometimes combined with paging.

questions.q: What types of caches are there, and which is better?
questions.st: Arm Cpu Verification New York New York interview
questions.a: Direct-mapped caches are fastest and simplest but suffer conflict misses; set-associative caches (2 to 16 ways) reduce conflicts at some cost in hit time and power; fully associative caches have no conflicts but are only practical when small (TLBs). Split versus unified, and write-back versus write-through, are other choices. No type is best in general: L1 caches favour low associativity for speed, while L2 and L3 favour higher associativity for hit rate.

questions.q: Why do we need virtual memory, and what are its advantages?
questions.st: Arm Cpu Verification Chandler Arizona interview
questions.a: Virtual memory lets programs use a large, contiguous address space independent of the physical memory size and layout. The advantages: isolation and protection between processes, more programs than fit in RAM (paging to disk), simpler linking and loading because every program can use the same addresses, shared memory and shared libraries, copy-on-write, and memory-mapped files.

questions.q: Why do we prefer a pipelined architecture over a non-pipelined one?
questions.st: ARM interview experience for verification engineer intern (on-campus, virtual)
questions.a: Pipelining raises throughput: with k stages, ideally one instruction completes every cycle instead of every k cycles, and each stage being shorter allows a higher clock. Hardware is also better used, because every stage is busy. The cost is hazards, extra registers and more complex control, but the performance gain is large, which is why every modern processor is pipelined.

questions.q: Why is MOESI better than MESI?
questions.st: Arm Verification Enablement Austin Texas interview

questions.q: With an n-bit address bus, how much memory can be accessed?
questions.st: Arm Verification Enablement Austin Texas interview
questions.a: An n-bit address bus can address 2^n locations. With byte addressing that is 2^n bytes: 16 bits give 64 KB, 32 bits give 4 GB, and 40 bits give 1 TB. If each address points to a wider word, multiply by the word size.

questions.q: A data path and a clock path are given, and one has extra latency. How would you correct it?
questions.st: Arm Verification Engineer New Delhi Delhi interview
questions.a: Balance the two paths. If the clock path has extra latency, the capture clock arrives late: that helps setup but hurts hold, so add delay on the data path (buffers) to fix hold, or reduce the skew by balancing the clock tree. If the data path has extra latency, it causes setup violations: shorten it (faster cells, restructuring, retiming, pipelining) or add useful skew by delaying the capture clock, provided the next stage's hold still passes.

questions.q: As the designer, how would you tell DV to test your block, and which signals must they check?
questions.st: Arm Asic Engineer Los Angeles California interview
questions.a: Give DV a specification that is testable: the features, the interface protocol and its timing, the registers, the error cases and the corner cases you are worried about (full, empty, overflow, reset in the middle of a transaction, back-pressure). List the outputs and internal status signals they must check, the invariants worth writing as assertions (handshakes, one-hot states, counters in range), and the coverage you expect. Review their test plan together.

questions.q: Can CPU clock speed increase indefinitely? Why not?
questions.st: Arm Hardware Engineer Intern United States interview
questions.a: No. Dynamic power grows with C V^2 f, and a higher frequency usually needs a higher voltage, so power and heat grow roughly with the cube of frequency (the power wall). Wire delay does not scale with transistor size, and shorter cycles mean more pipeline stages with larger branch penalties. Memory latency does not improve at the same rate, so a faster core just waits longer. That is why industry moved to more cores, wider and specialised units instead of higher clock rates.

questions.q: Describe power-management techniques.
questions.st: Arm Verification Engineer Canada interview
questions.a: Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) to match performance to load; clock gating to stop clocks to idle logic; power gating to switch off idle blocks with header or footer switches (with isolation and state retention); multiple voltage domains; multi-Vt cell selection to cut leakage; low-power states and sleep modes controlled by a power-management unit; and at software level, race-to-idle and scheduling. These are described in UPF or CPF for implementation and verification.

questions.q: Describe the components of a modern Arm mobile SoC and how they connect to each other.
questions.st: Arm Graduate Systems Architecture Engineer Cambridge Cambridgeshire interview
questions.a: A mobile SoC has clusters of Arm CPU cores (big and little), a GPU, an NPU for AI, a DSP and an image signal processor, video codecs, display and camera interfaces, a modem, security and boot blocks, a system cache, and memory controllers for LPDDR. They connect through a coherent interconnect (CCI or CMN using AMBA ACE/CHI) for the CPUs and IO-coherent masters, and AXI, AHB and APB buses for peripherals, with SMMUs for device address translation, plus clock, reset and power-management controllers.

questions.q: Describe the main components of a CPU.
questions.st: Arm Hardware Engineer Italy interview
questions.a: The control unit (fetch, decode, sequencing and branch handling), the datapath (register file, ALU, shifter, multiplier, FPU), pipeline registers, the program counter, load-store units with the memory interface, caches and TLBs, and in high-performance cores branch predictors, rename logic, reservation stations and a reorder buffer. Interrupt and exception logic and a bus interface connect it to the rest of the system.

questions.q: Design a simple parallel and a simple serial protocol.
questions.st: Arm Hardware Intern London England interview
questions.a: Parallel: data bus N bits wide, plus valid and ready (or req and ack); the sender drives data and valid, and a transfer happens on a clock edge when both valid and ready are high, so back-pressure is natural. Serial: one data line plus a clock (SPI-like) with a frame signal marking the start, shifting MSB first; or asynchronous like a UART with a start bit, N data bits, parity and a stop bit at an agreed baud rate. Discuss throughput, pin count, error detection and clock-domain issues.

questions.q: Discuss the design of an ARM processor.
questions.st: ARM interview experience for verification engineer intern (on-campus, virtual)
questions.a: A classic Arm core is a RISC load-store design: fixed-length 32-bit instructions (plus 16-bit Thumb), a large register file (31 general registers in AArch64), conditional execution or branches, and simple addressing modes, all of which make decode and pipelining easy. Implementations range from small in-order pipelines (Cortex-M, 3 stages) to wide out-of-order cores (Cortex-A and X) with branch prediction, renaming, multiple execution pipes, NEON SIMD, an MMU and caches, connected through AMBA buses.

questions.q: Draw a block diagram of a simple processor and show how an instruction flows through it.
questions.st: Arm Design And Verification Southampton Hampshire interview
questions.a: Draw the classic five stages: Fetch (PC addresses the instruction memory; PC + 4 or a branch target), Decode (read the register file, generate control signals, sign-extend the immediate), Execute (ALU operation or address calculation; branch comparison), Memory (load or store to the data memory), and Write-back (write the result to the register file). Follow one instruction, such as an add or a load, through each stage, showing the pipeline registers between stages and the forwarding paths.
